articles.description:
Olá, comunidade! 👋
Me chamo Gabriel Nandes, tenho 24 anos e essa é minha primeira aqui!
Atualmente curso o 1º semestre de Análise e Desenvolvimento de Sistemas na Universidade Cruzeiro do Sul, e resolvi começar a documentar minha jornada na área de tecnologia, tanto pra manter um registro de tudo que estou aprendendo, quanto pra trocar experiências com quem também está começando.
Um pouco sobre mim
Concilio a faculdade com o trabalho, o que tem me ensinado, na prática, organização e responsabilidade com processos. Atualmente atuo na WRA Import, e-commerce de brinquedos, motopeças e utilidades domésticas, como responsável pela área de envios na modalidade FULL, desde janeiro de 2026, liderando uma equipe de 2 pessoas. Antes disso, fui Auxiliar Financeiro na Zuup Tecnologia, na área de Governança Corporativa, lidando com contas a pagar e receber e pagamento de boletos, e atuei por 2 anos em atendimento ao cliente (cobrança e SAC) na GN Assessoria.
Essas experiências me deram uma base sólida em atenção a processos, organização e relacionamento com pessoas, além de um forte compromisso com prazos. Como pontos fortes, destaco também flexibilidade, facilidade de aprendizado, foco e atenção aos detalhes, além de inglês avançado, o que já tem ajudado bastante a acessar documentações técnicas e conteúdos internacionais da área.
Onde estou agora
Estou dando meus primeiros passos com lógica de programação, C e HTML5, e me preparando para os próximos módulos do curso: mais linguagens, banco de dados e desenvolvimento web/mobile.
Pretendo usar esse espaço pra compartilhar o que vou aprendendo pelo caminho, inclusive os erros e dificuldades, porque acho que isso ajuda tanto quanto os acertos!
Estou aberto a oportunidades de estágio em tecnologia, onde eu possa aplicar o que estou aprendendo e crescer junto com uma equipe.

articles.author: Saurav Pandey
articles.description:
No More Midnight Deploys: The Magic of Blue-Green Deployments


Imagine trying to upgrade the engine of a commercial airplane while it is mid-flight with passengers on board. In the software world, engineering teams face a similar challenge every day: they must update code, fix bugs, and release new features on live applications while millions of users are actively using them. This is where the concept of a blue-green deployment comes into play.
A blue-green deployment is a software release strategy that uses two identical hardware or cloud environments to minimize downtime and risk during updates. One environment, designated "Blue," runs the active, publicly accessible version of the application. The other environment, designated "Green," remains idle or hosts the new, upcoming version of…
articles.title: No More Midnight Deploys: The Magic of Blue-Green Deployments

Every frontend developer knows this pain: the backend isn't ready, it's down, or it returns data that doesn't match the design. You need to build UI against an API that doesn't exist yet.
The usual workarounds all have friction:
Spin up a mock server (json-server, mockoon) — another process, another port, another config to maintain.
Use a proxy tool — powerful, but heavy setup for a quick "give me this response" moment.
Edit your code — comment out the fetch, return hardcoded data, then remember to revert it before pushing.
DevTools Request blocking — blocks requests, but can't craft a response.
So I built Mokup: a Chrome DevTools panel that captures live API requests and turns them into editable mock rules. No proxy. No server. No code changes.

articles.author: Frank Hahanyu
articles.description:
INTRODUCTION


My first week at LuxDev Academy as a beginner in the tech field was awesome since all tutors gave us hands on tutoring , we covered installation of apps and understanding coding languages. For today I'll cover git workflow and all its components .
Version control can feel overwhelming when you first star writing code or managing data projects and for tools like git , they're designed to track changes in your projects over time using commands like git_add, git_commit, and git_push often feel like magic spells rather than logical steps.
To master or understand git you only need to understand the stages a file goes through during construction wich is :
This is where you do the work and it consists of the actual files on your computer's files system inside your project folder. In her when you create a new file or modify an existing code those changes only exist on your working directory, meaning git only notices that changes have occurred but it doesn't track or save them automatically and for that to happen we use git status 
The staging area acts as the intermediate step between your actual workspace and your saved history.
git add command , then you stage a specific file git add filename.py then stage all modified files at once git add
After the staging area we go ahead and commit to record those specific changes along with a clear descriptive message explaining what we updated( commit acts as a restore point).This is the commit prompt with a descriptive message i.e analysis data: git commit -m "add data analysis data"
git push origin main
Git gives you full control over how your project's history is recorded, organized and shared. You need to be keen with how you key in your prompts cause once you miss a step a lot of errors pile up and with that, once you understand these four stages then you won't have a problem working with Git in your work developments.
articles.title: GitHub Project :Understanding git work flow

articles.author: Yoan V
articles.description:
JOAN is an experimental, agent-native language and verification substrate. Real .joan source can be parsed, checked, formatted, compiled to deterministic bytecode, and executed in a bounded VM.
We are looking for three independent evaluators to run one small, reproducible GitHub-only task: safe repository metadata and instruction-file discovery.
git clone https://github.com/Yoanybx/joan.git
cd joan
git checkout 82f573c8e72927f1ee293cc9b3e7e5a2d6beeb41
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/absolute/path/outside/joan
bash scripts/run-adoption-trial.sh /absolute/path/to/new-output independent

Use independent only when that relationship is true. Otherwise use affiliated or undisclosed.
The task runtime is offline and read-only. It requires no JOAN account, API key, wallet, payment, server, telemetry, owner-host access, or listener. Cargo may download public dependencies during the build.
Preserve the generated JSON artifacts.
Record the SHA-256 of adoption-trial-run-receipt.json.
Submit the public Adoption trial report from the GitHub account that performed the evaluation.
State whether the task completed and whether you would repeat or recommend it for this bounded task.
Read the exact trial procedure and qualification boundary before running it.
JOAN is an alpha language preview, not a production release, host sandbox, or global network. This trial does not establish adoption, security completeness, or universal superiority over C. Negative results and reproducible bug reports are useful.
Repository: https://github.com/Yoanybx/joan
82f573c8e72927f1ee293cc9b3e7e5a2d6beeb41

articles.author: Voblit McVoblit
articles.description:
This is a tool which I think many will find useful. For a long time, calculators like the Ti84+CE have been stuck with a very limited and painfully slow python interpreter, if one was even provided, as non-python models do exist. But recently, I finished my tool that fixes this problem, by transpiling python to assembly!
While at first glance you may think the term "transpiler" is incorrect for a project like this, I decided to take a shortcut on the route, and effectively made a Python to C transpiler, like cython. Except here, I made it specifically target the CEdev toolchain, and call it to produce a .8xp program in result. Using plain Cython will be tough since it isn't really optimized.
Although it is very advanced, supporting lists, tuples, many data types, and a lot of programming structure types found in python and converting them to C, I do acknowledge the fact that it is still very limited on its I/O capabilities.
The github is here
articles.title: py2ez80: The Way To Put Python On The Ti84+CE

articles.author: Rulestack
articles.description:
Bluesky starter packs look like a single thing in the app — a shareable page that lets a new user follow a curated group in one tap. At the protocol level they are three separate records glued together by references, and if you create them from code (we do, as part of an automated outreach pipeline), the decomposition matters: it decides what you can update later, what you can only create once, and where a naive script will quietly make a mess.
Everything below is plain com.atproto.repo.createRecord / putRecord calls against your own PDS — no special API surface.
1. The list — app.bsky.graph.list. A starter pack is backed by an ordinary Bluesky list with purpose: app.bsky.graph.defs#referencelist. The list record itself holds metadata — name, purpose, createdAt, plus optional description a…
articles.title: Creating Bluesky starter packs from code: three AT Protocol records and one non-idempotency trap
